description:
Motivation: customers using the OpenAI-compatibility layer and the tool/function-calling endpoints were able to upload large multipart payloads and malformed parts which caused OOMs and destabilized streaming. This PR centralizes multipart validation into the API gateway handler and adds explicit per-part and total payload limits, content-type sniffing, and dual-field support for OpenAI-compat clients (accept both 'file' and 'files' form fields). The change is intentionally conservative: we validate before handing off to the streaming runtime so we can guarantee early rejection and deterministic error responses instead of mid-stream failures. Implementation highlights: 1) api/handlers/multipart_handler.py implements a two-pass scan: fast header-only pass to enforce per-part size and type heuristics, followed by a streaming handoff that preserves the original stream for allowed parts. 2) Introduced config flags (env) for PART_MAX_BYTES and MULTIPART_TOTAL_MAX_BYTES with sane defaults (10MB per part, 50MB total) and runtime metrics emitted for rejected uploads. 3) Content-type safety: we perform lightweight sniffing (magic bytes + declared header) to avoid accepting text/plain labeled binary blobs; for non-whitelisted types we respond 415 with structured error payload. 4) OpenAI-compat: map legacy form names and accept arrays and singletons to reduce client breakage. 5) Added unit and integration tests covering edge cases and a small e2e run that exercises the streaming generation + tool-call with an uploaded schema file. Checklist: - [x] Implement server-side validation and env flags - [x] Add metrics and structured error responses - [x] Add unit tests and integration e2e - [x] Update docs/compatibility and API reference - [x] Add a hotfix note for incident INT-4421 in changelog
[Evidence Passage 2 | Doc ID: dsid_ae068ee4aa9640159427cd941bef0238 | Chunk ID: dsid_ae068ee4aa9640159427cd941bef0238__c000 | Source: github | Title: add multipart/form-data handling, strict content-type validation, and payload limit enforcement for API tool/file inputs | Section: Overview]
description:
Motivation: users integrating tool/function calling and file uploads via the OpenAI-compatibility endpoints were sending a wide variety of content-types and very large multipart requests which caused inconsistent runtime behavior, high memory pressure, and unexpected acceptance of unsupported payloads. This PR introduces a focused, backwards-compatible implementation for multipart/form-data parsing on the OpenAI-compatibility path, strict Content-Type validation for tool/file inputs, and deterministic payload limits both per-file and per-request. Summary of changes: 1) Add a streaming-safe multipart parser that yields parts rather than buffering entire requests; 2) Validate Content-Type of each part (whitelist: text/*, image/*, application/json, application/octet-stream with explicit size checks); 3) Enforce configurable limits: max_file_size (default 10MiB), max_total_request_size (default 50MiB), max_parts_count (default 20). These defaults are conservative and documented; they can be overridden at tenant or route level via API config. 4) Hook validation into the OpenAI-compat layer so existing client integrations get predictable errors (400/413) with structured error bodies when inputs are rejected. 5) Add detailed unit and integration tests and end-to-end tests for streaming uploads and for the dedicated Dedicated/Private ingress paths. Backwards compatibility notes: this does not change the non-multipart JSON body semantics. Existing users who relied on accepting arbitrary large file uploads should update their tenant config or use Redwood Dedicated with higher quotas. Rollout plan: feature-flagged behind feature.enable_multipart_input (off by default); staged rollout to internal dogfood tenants, then gradual roll to 10%, 50%, 100% via config rollout. Checklist: - [x] Streaming-safe multipart parser implemented - [x] Content-Type whitelist + validation errors - [x] Per-file and per-request size enforcement + configurable defaults - [x] OpenAI-compa
[Evidence Passage 3 | Doc ID: dsid_ea298d9a235949febd7c03cb500817c4 | Chunk ID: dsid_ea298d9a235949febd7c03cb500817c4__c000 | Source: github | Title: Enforce MIME sniffing and chunking limits for tool/file uploads (OpenAI-compat layer) | Section: Overview]
description:
Motivation: Tool integrations and file attachments coming through the OpenAI-compatibility proxy were accepting overly permissive Content-Type headers and arbitrarily large streaming chunks which caused downstream model handlers to OOM or misclassify payloads. This PR adds deterministic MIME sniffing, per-tool attachment quotas, and streaming chunk size enforcement at the proxy layer so tool authors and user clients get immediate, deterministic rejections instead of opaque runtime errors.

What this changes: - Add a MIME sniffing pass for multipart and single-part uploads that normalizes Content-Type to a safe set and rejects unknown/binary blobs when a tool opts into textual input only. - Implement per-tool max_upload_bytes and max_chunks settings surfaced through the tools registry; defaults applied when not configured. - Enforce max_chunk_bytes for streaming/transfer-encoding style uploads so a single chunk cannot exceed safety limits. - Map legacy OpenAI style headers ("OpenAI-File-Name", "openai-content-type") into our normalized metadata to keep compatibility with existing clients. - Return structured JSON error payloads compatible with OpenAI-compat error shapes (error.code, error.message, error.type) so SDKs can handle programmatic failures. - Add unit and integration tests that exercise multipart boundaries, chunked streams, and header-based compatibility fallbacks.

Checklist: - [x] Add MIME sniffing implementation and canonicalizer in api/proxy/upload_validator.go - [x] Add per-tool config + defaults in services/tools/registry - [x] Add streaming chunk enforcement in streaming/handler.go - [x] Preserve OpenAI compatibility headers and map to internal metadata - [x] Add tests for multipart streaming, single-part file uploads, and header fallbacks - [x] Update docs: redwood-docs/api/file-uploads.md
[Evidence Passage 4 | Doc ID: dsid_fc5e896d8eb4455fa9b186d04e0845f4 | Chunk ID: dsid_fc5e896d8eb4455fa9b186d04e0845f4__c000 | Source: github | Title: catalog: surface model capability flags, pricing and limits for OpenAI-compat clients | Section: Overview]
description:
Motivation: Clients using the OpenAI-compat layer and our public model listing need a single, predictable surface to discover per-model capabilities (streaming stability, function/tool-calling support, structured-output specializations) and unit economics (pricing per token, soft/hard limits and concurrency). This PR extends the model catalog API and internal catalog objects to include capability and pricing metadata, plus server-side filters that power the console and SDKs.

Summary of changes: added explicit capability flags (openai_compat, supports_streaming_stable, supports_function_calling, structured_output_profiles) to the model listing; exposed priced_units and limits metadata (cost_per_input_token, cost_per_output_token, max_tokens_per_request, recommended_concurrency, rate_limit_tier). Implemented new query params for the GET /v1/models endpoint to filter by capability, max_estimated_cost_per_k, min_stability_score, region, and quantization support. Updated the OpenAI compatibility layer to prefer models with openai_compat=true for compatibility endpoints and to fall back predictably to compatible variants when a requested capability is not available. Added docs, SDK bindings, and tests.

Why this is safe: fields are additive. No breaking schema changes for existing consumers. Default behavior for compatibility endpoints is unchanged unless clients explicitly query the new fields or filtering. We included a migration path for older model entries missing cost metadata (defaults used and surfaced as "unknown").

What are the default size limits for file uploads and total request size for the new multipart upload support on the OpenAI-compatible API endpoints?

Overview
This playbook centralizes Redwood's company-wide operational policies for onboarding people and services, managing access and permissions, authorizing changes, governing data lifecycles, running procurement and expenses, onboarding vendors, and standardizing travel approvals. The intent is to provide a single, actionable reference for managers, security, legal, finance, and engineering teams.

Scope
Applies to: all Redwood employees, contractors, and vendors that require access to systems or handle company data. The procedures below are mandatory unless an approved exception is recorded in Risk and Exceptions.

Principles
- Least privilege by default.
- Separation of duties for sensitive approvals.
- Time-boxed, auditable changes.
- Risk-based procurement and vendor due diligence.
- Clear owner and SLAs for operational requests.

1) Access & Permissions
Summary: Access requests, role assignments, and privileged elevation must follow the centralized flow so we keep IAM clean and auditable.

Owner: Identity and Access team (eng-infra) | Request queue: OPS-AUTH
SLA: Standard role requests: 48 business hours. Privileged (root/keyholder) access: 5 business days with an approved justification. Emergency access: documented within 24 hours post-event.

Process (standard requests):
1. User submits request via OPS-AUTH with reason, duration, and target resource (include ticket tag: AUTH-REQ-<team>).
2. Manager approves (first approver).
3. System owner (team that owns resource) approves (second approver) for non-privileged roles; for privileged roles, Security review is required.
4. Identity team applies RBAC change and documents the grant in the ticket.
5. Access is time-limited where possible; automation sends expiration reminders 7 days before.

Privileged Access Controls:
- Multi-person attestation every 90 days for privileged accounts.
- MFA required for all privileged logins.
- Session recording enabled for admin consoles where supported.

- Quarterly access attestation: team owners must validate active entitlements and remove stale accounts. Failure to respond triggers automated revocation notices.

Governance Principles and Procedures

Short summary
This document defines the company-wide principles and operational procedures for access and permissions, change management, data classification and handling, procurement and expenses, vendor management, travel, and the set of internal templates teams must use. It is the canonical reference for policy owners, approvers, and reviewers.

Scope
Applies to: all employees, contractors, and vendors with access to Redwood systems or customer data. Covers: corporate systems, production infrastructure, third-party services, and travel/expense processes. Does NOT replace team-level runbooks for technical operations; instead it provides the governance layer and mandatory integration points (tickets, approvals, audit evidence).

Governance principles (company-wide)
- Least privilege: Access is granted at the minimum permission level required for the task. Role-based access patterns must be used where possible.
- Separation of duties: No single individual should both request and approve a high-risk procurement, or both deploy and review their own production change.
- Auditability: All privileged operations, purchases, and vendor onboarding actions must have an auditable ticket or contract reference.
- Risk-based controls: Controls scale with data sensitivity and financial exposure. Higher sensitivity or spend requires more reviews and security evidence.
- Time-boxed approvals: Standard requests should have target SLAs (see sections below). Escalations must be documented.

h2. When to use this runbook
Use this runbook when a serving-runtime change must be shipped quickly to mitigate an active incident (typically Sev-1). This covers code change, build, validation, and handoff to rollout owners.

h2. Preconditions
* Emergency change approvals recorded per /policies-and-process/change-management/emergency-change-policy-v3
* Incident channel exists (or a dedicated Slack thread) with IC identified
* A rollback plan exists (previous runtime image tag + restart procedure)

h2. Step 1 — Cut a hotfix branch
1. Create branch naming: hotfix/runtime-<YYYYMMDD>-<short-issue>
2. Cherry-pick the minimum fix commit(s) only.
3. Update CHANGELOG entry under 'Runtime Hotfixes'.

h2. Step 2 — Create PR and get emergency reviews
1. Open GitHub PR targeting release branch (preferred) or main if release branch is not available.
2. Required reviewers: runtime on-call + SRE on-call (or IC).
3. Include in PR description: incident link, hypothesis, risk, rollback, rollout owners.

h2. Step 3 — Build + sign artifacts
Follow /eng-infra/ci-cd-and-build/hotfix-build-and-signing. Minimum artifacts:
* runtime container image (multi-arch if applicable)
* SBOM (CycloneDX)
* provenance attestation

h2. Step 4 — Validate the fix
*Minimum* validation required even in an incident:
* Unit tests for affected module
* One perf-canary run for representative model (e.g., Llama 3.1 70B)
* One stress test at the incident-triggering pattern (sequence length + concurrency)

Validation checklist (record results in PR):
* Error rate improves or eliminates the triggering error
* p95 latency does not regress > 10% compared to previous runtime image for the same workload
* No increase in OOM or GPU reset counters

h2. Step 5 — Prepare rollout notes
In the incident channel, post:
* New runtime image tag
* Expected impact during rollout (restarts, brief connection resets)
* Canary target (Hosted region or Dedicated cluster)
* Rollback criteria (metrics + customer symptom)
[Evidence Passage 2 | Doc ID: dsid_452dc45d76754cbca8a3674170599633 | Chunk ID: dsid_452dc45d76754cbca8a3674170599633__c001 | Source: confluence | Title: Emergency Change Policy (Production) — v3 | Section: *Service Owner* (or delegate) for the component being changed]
# *Service Owner* (or delegate) for the component being changed

Additional approvals based on scenario:
* Security-related or suspected exploit: *Security on-call*
* Customer-visible behavior change (responses/routing/model selection): *Product on-call* or responsible PM
* Any change requiring customer maintenance coordination (Dedicated/Private): *Customer Success escalation manager*

h2. Minimum checklist
Record in ticket/PR/incident timeline:
* Hypothesis for the fix
* Blast radius (Hosted regions; Dedicated clusters/customers; model families)
* Rollback plan with explicit trigger (metric or customer symptom)
* Risk assessment: data integrity, security, performance
* What is changing (code vs config vs infra)
* Owner for post-change monitoring

h2. Documentation and audit requirements
* Create/link a ticket (Linear preferred; Jira acceptable).
* Open a GitHub PR (even if fast-tracked) OR link to an existing PR and commit SHA.
* Record approvals in PR review, incident thread, or change record comment.
* Update incident timeline with: start time, change time, outcome.

h2. Rollout constraints
* Use a canary wherever possible (one Hosted region or a single Dedicated cluster) before broad rollout.
* If canary is not possible, document why and get IC sign-off.
* Do not deploy unrelated changes under one emergency change record.

h2. Post-change requirements
Within 2 business days:
* Create follow-up in incident review (root cause, change made, why it worked).
* Document any deviations from normal release procedures and corrective actions.
* Remove any temporary flags/throttles (owner + deadline).

h2. Purpose
Dedicated customers run on isolated clusters with customer-specific SLOs and maintenance expectations. This page describes how to roll out an emergency runtime hotfix to Dedicated clusters safely and with required customer coordination.

h2. Key differences vs Hosted
* Customers may have pinned model versions and strict latency SLOs.
* Maintenance windows may be contractually required.
* Failover between clusters may not exist; assume restarts can cause brief interruptions.

h2. Required inputs
Before scheduling a Dedicated hotfix rollout, gather:
* Customer name + cluster ID
* Current runtime image tag
* Target runtime image tag
* Impact statement (expected restart behavior)
* Rollback image tag
* Whether the issue is customer-specific or global

h2. Required approvals
* IC or SRE on-call approval for emergency change
* Dedicated service owner approval
* Customer Success escalation manager sign-off on customer messaging

h2. Customer communication requirements
For Sev-1: follow /oncall-and-incident-response/incident-process/sev1-communication-requirements. Additionally for Dedicated hotfixes:
* If we will restart runtime pods: send a short note that brief interruptions may occur
* Provide a time window (even if approximate)
* Provide rollback criteria in plain language (e.g., 'if errors increase after deployment, we will revert within 15 minutes')

h2. Rollout plan
1. Canary on one Dedicated cluster first (prefer: internal dogfood dedicated or lowest-traffic customer, with CSEM approval).
2. Validate for 30 minutes: success rate, p95 latency, GPU OOM, restart frequency, customer-specific health checks.
3. Schedule remaining impacted clusters; do not roll more than 3 clusters in parallel unless IC approves.

Avoid:
* Overly specific internal details (hostnames, precise exploit details)
* Blaming language

h2. Dedicated-specific communication
If impact is isolated to one or more Dedicated clusters:
* CSEM must notify impacted customers directly (email + optional call).
* Include: whether a maintenance action is required (e.g., rolling runtime restart), expected duration, and whether customer traffic will fail over.
* If a hotfix rollout is planned, provide the rollout window and the rollback criteria in customer-friendly terms.

maya: Quick sync — we keep seeing orphaned sampled spans when late enrichment attaches billing keys. How do we want to handle reassembling sampled traces across the ingest pipeline?
aj: Can you paste a short example of the orphan pattern you saw?
maya: Sure. flow: edge -> service A (sample=1) -> service B (not-sampled) -> enrichment service adds billing_key later. Because B dropped spans, when we stitch by trace_id the sampled span arrives first and enrichment comes with billing later so cost attribution misses.
aj: So it's a timing/ordering issue, not missing IDs.
lee: Two quick approaches: 1) attach a small "sampled_marker" envelope at the edge that persists until enrichment joins; 2) make enrichment do a lookup against recent sampled trace set. Tradeoffs in storage + latency.
chris: Option 1 sounds cheaper on CPU but increases ingress size and retention window. Option 2 adds a query per enrich event, which could spike QPS.
olivia: Also consider route-level batching: if enrichment is delayed only slightly, a short-lived in-memory cache (LRU with TTL) in the enrichment consumer might be enough.
maya: TTL needs to be tuned: we observed delays up to 45s in some backfills and retries. LRU+45s = lot of memory on hot pods.
aj: Could be sharded by tenant. Hot tenants pay the memory cost; cold tenants have best-effort reassembly.
lee: We also discussed keeping a compact index in Kafka for sampled trace headers: a tiny topic keyed by trace_id with last-seen timestamp and sampled_marker. Enrichment could do an async read (lightweight) using the Kafka log via RocksDB local store (like a changelog). More operational complexity but bounded storage.
chris: That aligns with our stream-processing mindset. But we need idempotency: race where marker written after enrichment read.
maya: We can have enrichment write a tombstone if it can't find marker, then a reconciler job can sweep tombstones and reconcile with late markers — but that adds another background job and potential double-counting windows.
olivia: For cost attribution correctness we need deterministic rules. Suggestion: attribution rule = if any sampled_marker seen within window W of the span timestamp, attribute to sampled cohort; otherwise default.
aj: Define W = 2 minutes for now as a configurable knob per tenant. Longer window increases false positives.
lee: Implementation sketch in protos:

message SamplingMarker {
  string trace_id = 1;
  int64 ts_ms = 2;
  string tenant_id = 3;
}

and a compact store that holds only (trace_id -> ts_ms, bitflags) for W.
chris: Operational questions: retention sizing math, cross-az replication, and metrics to detect when enrichment misses markers (i.e., leakage signal).
maya: Metrics we need: marker_emitted, marker_lookup_hit, marker_lookup_miss, reconcilations_run, attribution_delta_percent. Also a tag metric by tenant.
olivia: For rollout: 1) emit markers at edge for a small % of traffic (canary) 2) run enrichment lookup in shadow read path and record hits/misses 3) switch attribution for canary tenants 4) expand.
aj: Can we avoid changing SDKs at edge? We can inject marker in proxy sidecar or edge lambda so most customers unaffected.
lee: SDK change optional. Proxy + edge-router is ideal — single place.
chris: Also add a debug flag to force emit for a trace_id for offline repro: `X-Debug-Sample: force-marker`.
maya: Action items: 
- (maya) write short RFC with the two designs (compact Kafka-changelog store vs enrichment LRU) and cost math. Due EOD Thursday.
- (aj) prototype shadow lookup in enrichment consumer (1 day).
- (lee) sizing calc for W=15s, 45s, 120s and tenant percentiles (1 day).
- (olivia) define metrics + dashboards (alerts for miss rate > 0.5% for top 10 tenants).
- (chris) propose reconciliation approach if we get significant late joins (investigate tombstone reconciler complexity).

maya: Anything else?
aj: Can we add simulated load to perf-test the RocksDB local lookup latency? I'll add to perf board.
lee: FYI edge-proxy team already has a hook to add small headers, I'll talk to them.
olivia: SGTM. I'll draft the dashboard panels and SLIs.
chris: If we need to avoid budget surprises, we can start with a very small canary tenant set and keep a tight W.
maya: Thanks all — I'll post the RFC link here once it's up. :thumbsup:

Runbook: immediate triage and remediation (oncall/SRE)
1) Detect and classify (5 minutes)
   - Check dashboards: slot-coordinator ticket wait-time, fanout-orch reassembly latency, KVCache hit-rate.
   - Run quick queries: `SELECT count(*) FROM tracing.events WHERE service='fanout-orch' AND span='reassembly' AND duration>100`
2) If Mode A (kernel saturation):
   a) Apply emergency admission control: `POST /slot-coordinator/v1/emergency-policy` with body { "mode": "restrict-fanout", "max_subrequests": 2 }
   b) Trigger selective fallback for heavy tenants: add `fallback:true` tag via `/fanout-orch/v1/tags/update` for tenant ids causing > 20% of queued tickets.
   c) If sustained > 30m, escalate to infra-oncall for capacity add or hot-patch kernel flattening.
3) If Mode B (KVCache eviction storm):
   a) Run `kvcache-proxy diagnostics warmup --prefix <affected-prefix>` and collect `evict_histogram` and `warmup_latency` logs.
   b) Temporarily increase cache retention policy for affected partition: `PATCH /kvcache-config { "eviction_window_ms": 600000 }` (owner approval required).
   c) If data loss suspected, enable controlled shadow-warmup from shadow-cluster for 15m.
4) If Mode C (reassembly deadlock):
   a) Use diagnostic endpoint: `GET /fanout-orch/debug/blocked-requests` to list stuck correlation ids.
   b) For each stuck id, trigger a controlled abort and reissue using fallback policy: `POST /fanout-orch/admin/reissue?correlation_id=...&fallback=atomic`
   c) Schedule a post-incident test to replay 1,000 affected traces with the synthetic harness (see Benchmarking protocol below).
